newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Some Bosnians resent Diana on mine crusade.
newsitem.headline: Some Bosnians resent Diana on mine crusade.

text.p: Princess Diana may have melted the hearts of landmine survivors in central Bosnia, but in Sarajevo her visit went at best unnoticed, at worst resented by local people.
"Yet another visitor to the zoo," said Sanja, an unemployed doctor, when asked what she thought of Diana's weekend visit to Bosnia as part of her crusade against landmines.
"I have no interest in her visit whatsoever."

The aim of Diana's mission is something all Bosnians agree with -- ridding the country of more than a million landmines which are maiming or killing up to three people a week. Experts estimate 150,000 mines will still be in the ground in 20 years' time.
The cavalcade of buses and cars carrying British press and police around with Diana has only perplexed local Bosnians, many of whom do not even know who she is.
Unlike the royalty-obsessed British tabloids, state television in Bosnia gave Diana's trip only a brief mention at the very end of the main evening news.
Many Bosnians, concerned about whether their country's fragile peace will hold, have little time for a glamorous princess being photographed with victims.
"Yet another world-famous face visiting Bosnia. Where was she when the mines were planted?" one woman asked.
Diana has made no comment during this "private visit", though it is likely to raise awareness of the problem outside the country and funds for mine-clearing efforts.
Maja, an architect, said she was more excited about plans for the city's first major rock concert in peacetime by the band U2 in September.

"U2 will give a concert here as in any other normal city. We are fed up with humanitarian tourists who come and go, taking pictures of themselves in our ruins. At least the U2 concert will help us feel normal and equal to others."

One angry female pensioner said she was almost furious when she saw Diana on the news on Friday. "They are parading around while we don't even get pensions...She could send a million dollars if she wanted to help, instead of parading here."
Samir, an engineer working for an international organisation, said Diana's visit would be worthwhile only if she managed to raise money for removing mines.
"She came on a noble mission, no doubt, but...it is the mission itself that matters, not her personality.

"Why does nobody report about our reconstruction projects or the return of refugees? These are important things for us. Her visit matters only so far as she has brought some money for landmine clearance."
